title: MANY ARE CALLED. FEW ARE CHOSEN. AND THAT SHOULD TERRIFY THE PERSON WHO ONLY LOOKS CHRISTIAN.
paragraphs:
MANY ARE CALLED. FEW ARE CHOSEN. AND THAT SHOULD TERRIFY THE PERSON WHO ONLY LOOKS CHRISTIAN.
The Warning Jesus Hid in Plain Sight—and Why the Wedding Garment Changes Everything
There are words of Jesus that comfort you.
And then there are words of Jesus that refuse to let you sleep comfortably.
“Many are called, but few are chosen.”
We print verses about grace on coffee mugs. We underline promises of peace. We share Scriptures about blessing when life becomes unbearable.
But this sentence?
This sentence follows you into the quiet.
Because Jesus did not say it to atheists mocking Him from a distance.
He said it at the end of a story about people who had been invited to a wedding.
People who had heard the call.
People who were close enough to the celebration to know that something important was happening.
And one man even made it inside.
That is where the warning becomes frightening.
You can be near holy things and still not belong to Christ.
You can know Christian vocabulary.
You can sing worship songs.
You can repost Bible verses.
You can sit in church until the preacher recognizes your face.
You can know when to say “Amen.”
You can look spiritually alive to everybody watching you...
and still have a heart that has never truly surrendered to the King.
Jesus ends His parable in Matthew 22:14 with these Greek words:
Πολλοὶ γάρ εἰσιν κλητοί, ὀλίγοι δὲ ἐκλεκτοί.
Polloi gar eisin klētoi, oligoi de eklektoi.
“For many are called, but few are chosen.”
The word κλητοί — klētoi carries the idea of those who are called or invited.
The word ἐκλεκτοί — eklektoi means chosen, selected, elect.
But if we isolate that sentence from the story Jesus just told, we can easily turn a terrifyingly beautiful Gospel warning into something Jesus was not saying.
So go back to the banquet.
Jesus describes a king who prepared a wedding feast for his son.
Already, the picture matters.
A king.
A son.
A wedding.
An invitation.
A feast prepared at tremendous cost.
And messengers sent to tell the invited guests:
Come.
Everything is ready.
But they would not come.
Think about the insanity of that.
The king was not asking starving people to provide the meal.
The feast had already been prepared.
They simply had to respond to the invitation.
Yet some were indifferent.
One went to his farm.
Another went to his business.
Others became violently hostile toward the king’s servants.
Different reactions.
Same rejection.
Some hated the invitation.
Others were simply too busy for it.
And perhaps that second group should frighten modern Christians even more.
Because not everybody rejects Christ by shaking a fist toward heaven.
Some reject Him by being perpetually distracted.
Work.
Money.
Relationships.
Entertainment.
Ambition.
Notifications.
Pleasure.
Another episode.
Another purchase.
Another promotion.
Another tomorrow.
Nothing necessarily looks dramatic.
Nobody announces, “I reject Jesus Christ.”
They simply keep living as though the King’s invitation can wait.
And one day they discover that eternity did not wait with them.
Jesus said elsewhere:
“What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world and forfeits his soul?”
You can succeed at almost everything people applaud...
and fail at the one thing eternity exposes.
But then the parable takes an astonishing turn.
The original invitees reject the king, so the servants are sent out into the roads.
Bring whoever you find.
Matthew deliberately tells us that they gathered “both bad and good.”
Do not rush past those words.
Bad and good.
Suddenly the wedding hall begins filling with people who may never have imagined themselves sitting at the king’s table.
This is where scandal begins turning into grace.
The unwanted can come.
The morally disgraced can come.
The person with a past can come.
The person whose family knows exactly what he did can come.
The woman carrying memories she wishes she could erase can come.
The addict can come.
The hypocrite who finally admits his hypocrisy can come.
The religious person who discovers that religion cannot save him can come.
The ashamed can come.
The broken can come.
The guilty can come.
The person reading this article while secretly wondering, “After everything I have done, could Jesus possibly still want me?” can come.
The invitation goes into the streets.
Grace goes looking where respectable people sometimes refuse to go.
This is Christianity.
Not bad people pretending they became good enough for God.
It is guilty people being summoned to a feast they could never have earned.
But then Jesus introduces one guest who should make every reader examine his own heart.
The king enters.
He sees a man without a wedding garment.
“Friend,” the king asks, “how did you get in here without a wedding garment?”
And Scripture says:
ὁ δὲ ἐφιμώθη.
Ho de ephimōthē.
“But he was speechless.”
The verb carries the force of being silenced—muzzled, left without an answer.
No excuse.
No argument.
No defense.
He had entered the celebration, but he was unprepared for the king.
And here we must be careful.

Christians have interpreted the wedding garment in several related ways across the history of the Church. Some emphasize the righteousness God provides; others emphasize the transformed life appropriate to those who genuinely respond to God’s invitation. We should not force one small detail of a parable beyond what Scripture permits.
But the central warning is unmistakable:
Being around the kingdom is not the same as belonging to the King.
An outward response without inward reality will not survive divine examination.
That truth appears repeatedly in the teaching of Jesus.
“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven.”
Notice what those people call Him.
Lord.
They possess religious language.
They even point toward impressive spiritual works.
Yet Jesus warns that outward profession by itself is not saving faith.
This should destroy one of the most dangerous lies in modern Christianity:
“I’m probably okay.”
Probably?
Your soul is too valuable for probably.
“I believe in God.”
James reminds us that even demons believe that God is one—and shudder.
“I grew up Christian.”
Jesus never said, “You must grow up Christian.”
He said:
“You must be born again.”
“I go to church.”
Wonderful.
But entering a church building cannot reconcile a sinner to God any more than entering a hospital lobby makes someone a physician.
“I’m a good person.”
Compared with whom?
Your neighbor?
Your ex?
The criminal on television?
The standard is not the worst person you know.
The standard is the holiness of God.
And that is exactly why the Gospel is such spectacular news.
Because Christianity does not announce that you can climb high enough to reach God.
It announces that God came down to rescue sinners.
Jesus Christ did not enter history merely to make decent people slightly nicer.
The eternal Son of God took on flesh.
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He went willingly toward a Roman cross.
And there, the sinless One suffered for sinners.
Isaiah had written centuries earlier:
כֻּלָּנוּ כַּצֹּאן תָּעִינוּ
Kullānu ka-tzon ta‘inu.
“All we like sheep have gone astray.”
Then comes the breathtaking turn:
וַיהוָה הִפְגִּיעַ בּוֹ אֵת עֲוֹן כֻּלָּנוּ
The LORD laid upon Him the iniquity of us all.
Our sin.
His suffering.
Our guilt.
His sacrifice.
Our rebellion.
His wounds.
And the cross was not the end.
Jesus rose from the dead.
The tomb could not keep Him.
Death could not defeat Him.
Sin did not have the final word.
And your scandal does not have to have the final word either.
That is why the Gospel is not self-improvement.
It is rescue.
It is not Jesus helping you decorate your old life with religious language.
It is Christ calling you to repent, believe, die to the old master, and walk in newness of life.
The Greek New Testament uses the word μετάνοια — metanoia, repentance.
Biblical repentance is deeper than feeling embarrassed because consequences finally arrived.
It is a Spirit-awakened turning of the heart toward God.
It says:
I have sinned.
I cannot save myself.
I will stop defending what Christ died to forgive.
Jesus, have mercy on me.
And this is where “many are called, but few are chosen” must not be twisted into despair.
Jesus is not telling broken sinners, “Become worthy enough and perhaps God will let you into the banquet.”
Look again at the story.
The banquet was prepared by the king.
The invitation originated with the king.
The servants were sent by the king.
The undeserving were gathered because the king commanded that they be brought in.
Grace starts with God.
Salvation is not your trophy for becoming impressive.
Paul writes that by grace you have been saved through faith, and that this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works, so nobody can boast.
But the grace that saves us is not permission to remain comfortably married to the sin from which Christ came to rescue us.
Grace does not say, “Keep your idols. Keep your secret rebellion. Keep Christ as an accessory.”
Grace says:
Come home.
The door is open because Someone paid the price.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Maybe behind the version of you everybody sees is another version nobody knows.
You know exactly which browser history you keep deleting.
You know the bitterness you keep feeding.
You know the relationship you know dishonors God.
You know the money you worship.
You know how carefully you manufacture your Christian appearance.
You know the unforgiveness.
The secret messages.
The hidden addiction.
The pride.
The envy.
The lust.
The compromise.
The prayerlessness.
The spiritual exhaustion.
The strange emptiness that arrives when everybody else has gone to bed and there is nobody left to impress.
And perhaps your greatest fear is not that God does not see it.
Your greatest fear is that He does.
He does.
And here is what might break you:
He is still calling you.
Not because your sin is insignificant.
The cross proves that sin is devastatingly serious.
But the same cross proves that the mercy of God is greater than anything repentance brings into the light.
Peter denied Jesus.
Three times.
Imagine the shame when the rooster crowed.
Peter had insisted that even if everyone else abandoned Christ, he would remain.
Then fear exposed him.
“I do not know the man.”
Imagine having that sentence trapped inside your memory after Jesus is crucified.
Peter could have believed his worst moment had become his permanent name.
Failure.
Coward.
Denier.
Scandal.
But resurrection morning changed the vocabulary.
Jesus restored Peter.
Grace did not pretend the denial never happened.
Grace rewrote what the denial would ultimately mean.
Peter's failure was real.
Christ's mercy was greater.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel Warrior message:
Not because consequences always disappear.
Not because repentance makes history imaginary.
Not because Christianity teaches us to call evil good.
Jesus rewrites everything because the sinner who comes to Him in repentant faith is no longer required to be defined by the darkest chapter of his past.
“There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”
ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ — en Christō Iēsou.
In Christ Jesus.
Those three words change everything.
The question is not whether you have scandal in your story.
We all carry the stain of sin.
The question is:
Are you in Christ?
Not merely around Christians.
Not merely familiar with Christianity.
Not merely emotionally moved by Jesus.
Not merely following Christian pages.
Not merely baptized while living as your own god.
Not merely wearing the vocabulary.
Are you His?
Because eventually the King enters the room.
That is the uncomfortable part of Matthew 22 we cannot remove to make Christianity easier to market.
There is judgment.
There is accountability.
There is an eternity beyond the grave.
Jesus Himself speaks of outer darkness and weeping and gnashing of teeth.
The same Jesus who welcomed children warned adults about judgment.
The same Jesus who touched lepers called sinners to repentance.
The same Jesus who forgave the guilty warned religious hypocrites.
The same Jesus who went to the cross will also return as King.
Biblical love does not erase His warnings.
Biblical love believes Him.
So do not turn this article into another emotional moment you forget by dinner.
Examine yourself.
Not obsessively staring at whether you have performed enough good works to purchase salvation.
Look to Christ.
Ask whether your hope rests in Him.
Ask whether your profession of faith is accompanied by the evidence of a heart being transformed by His grace.
When you fall, do you run toward Christ in repentance or hide from Him while protecting the sin?
Do you want Jesus Himself—or merely the benefits you hope He will give you?
Would you still want Christ if following Him cost you the approval of people you desperately want to impress?
Those questions are uncomfortable.
Let them be.
Eternity is too important for comfortable lies.
And if something inside you is whispering, “It is too late for me,” remember the thief beside Jesus.
He had no lifetime left to repair his reputation.
No decades available for religious achievement.
No opportunity to build an impressive Christian résumé.
He had a dying body, a guilty history, and Christ beside him.
He turned toward Jesus.
“Remember me.”
And Jesus answered with paradise.
That is grace.
But notice something else.
The thief did not say, “My sin does not matter.”
He acknowledged his guilt.
He recognized Christ.
He entrusted himself to the King.
That is the difference between cheap religious comfort and saving grace.
Saving grace brings sinners home to Jesus.
So if this has exposed something you have been hiding, do not perform for the comments.
But do not hide from God either.
If you need brothers and sisters in Christ to pray for you, simply write:
Pray.
We need fewer audiences and more brothers and sisters.
It cannot.
But if Christ has given us good news, we should not be ashamed to carry it.
Someone connected to you may never enter a church this week.
They may never open a Bible today.
But they might stop because you shared this.
Send it privately to the friend whose faith has grown cold.
Not so we can build a crowd around a page.
So we can keep pointing the crowd toward Christ.
It does not.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
before you share...
before you comment...
before you tag anybody...
settle the question that matters infinitely more than all of them:
What have you done with the invitation of the King?
Because one day your follower count will not matter.
Your bank balance will not matter.
The house will belong to someone else.
The trophies will collect dust.
The clothes will be discarded.
The notifications will stop.
Someone else will eventually sit at your desk.
And the world that seemed incapable of continuing without you...
will continue.
But you will meet God.
On that day, Christianity will no longer be content.
Jesus will no longer be a subject for debate.
Eternity will no longer be theoretical.
And “many are called, but few are chosen” will no longer be merely a verse you once read on Facebook.
So hear the invitation while you can hear it.
Come to Christ.
Come honestly.
Come guilty.
Come ashamed.
Come tired.
Come without pretending.
Repent and believe the Gospel.
Do not wait until you become worthy.
You cannot make yourself worthy of grace—that is why it is grace.
Bring Christ the chapter you thought destroyed your story.
Bring Him the failure.
Bring Him the addiction.
Bring Him the pride.
Bring Him the secret.
Bring Him the religious mask.
Bring Him the years you wasted.
Bring Him the heart you cannot repair.
And trust the crucified and risen Savior who receives sinners.
The warning is real.
Judgment is real.
Sin is real.
But so is the cross.
So is the empty tomb.
So is forgiveness.
So is grace.
And so is Jesus.
But never confuse supporting the messenger with responding to the Message.
A share cannot save you.
A comment cannot save you.
A church membership cannot save you.
Your reputation cannot save you.
Your good works cannot erase your guilt.
Jesus saves.
And perhaps the most terrifying tragedy is not that the invitation was never sent...
but that it arrived again and again, while someone kept assuming there would always be another tomorrow.
Do not merely admire the invitation to the wedding feast—make sure your heart has truly bowed before the King.
